title: Achior
lead: The Ammonite leader in the book of Judith who tells Holofernes the truth about Israel's God, is handed over to the besieged town of Bethulia, and at the end is circumcised and joins the house of Israel. He stands in a line of foreigners who recognize Israel's God, from Jethro and Rahab to Ruth and Naaman.

sections.b: Achior is "the leader of all the Ammonites" in Holofernes' army (Judith 5:5). Asked who the Israelites are, he tells their history from Abraham to the return from exile and warns that they cannot be beaten unless they sin against their God (Judith 5:5–21). Holofernes mocks him as a prophet for hire and sends him to share Bethulia's fate (Judith 6:2–13), but the town welcomes him (Judith 6:14–21). When Judith returns with Holofernes' head, Achior faints, honors her, believes in God, is circumcised and is "joined to the house of Israel" (Judith 14:6–10).

Deuteronomy bars Ammonites and Moabites from "the assembly of the LORD," even to the tenth generation (Deuteronomy 23:3–6), and Nehemiah enforced it (Nehemiah 13:1–3). Ruth the Moabite, ancestor of David, stands on the other side (Ruth 1:16; Ruth 4:13–17), as does the promise that foreigners who hold to God's covenant will be gathered with Israel (Isaiah 56:3–7). Achior's conversion (Judith 14:10) takes Ruth's side. The Mishnah records a debate over Judah, an Ammonite convert, who was admitted because the nations had been mixed since Sennacherib (Mishnah Yadayim 4:4).

sections.h: A foreigner who speaks the truth
sections.b: Like Balaam, who was hired to curse Israel and could only bless it (Numbers 22–24), Achior is called a prophet for hire by those who wanted another answer (Judith 6:2; Judith 6:5). Like Jethro (Exodus 18:10–11), Rahab (Joshua 2:9–11) and Naaman (2 Kings 5:15), he confesses Israel's God after seeing what God has done. Christian commentators have read him as a figure of the Gentiles who come to faith.
